facts.text: A cat's purr vibrates at a frequency between 25 and 150 hertz, which studies suggest can help heal bones and reduce pain, in both the cat and nearby humans.
Dogs can smell roughly ten thousand to one hundred thousand times better than humans, thanks to having up to 300 million scent receptors compared to our 6 million.
A group of kittens born to the same mother can actually have different fathers, a phenomenon called superfecundation that happens more often than most people realize.
Dogs curl up in a ball to sleep as an instinct from their wild ancestors, conserving body heat and protecting vital organs from predators.
Cats spend nearly a third of their waking hours grooming themselves, which helps regulate body temperature, remove parasites, and keep their scent hidden from predators.
A dog's nose print is unique, just like a human fingerprint, with a pattern of ridges and creases that no two dogs share.
Cats can rotate their ears independently up to 180 degrees, using up to 32 muscles to precisely pinpoint the exact direction of a sound.
Puppies are born completely deaf and blind, relying entirely on smell and touch for the first couple of weeks of their lives.
A cat's whiskers are roughly as wide as its body, helping it judge in an instant whether it can fit through a narrow gap.
Dogs experience a rush of oxytocin, the same bonding hormone released between mothers and babies, simply from making eye contact with their owner.
Cats have a special reflective layer behind their retina called the tapetum lucidum, which is why their eyes seem to glow in the dark.
A dog's sense of time seems to be based on scent fading, which may be part of how they know roughly how long you've been gone.
Kittens start purring within just a few days of being born, often while nursing, likely as a way to signal contentment to their mother.
Dogs can be trained to detect changes in human blood sugar or oncoming seizures purely through subtle shifts in scent, sometimes minutes before symptoms appear.
A cat's rough tongue is covered in tiny backward-facing hooks called papillae, which work like a built-in hairbrush and help scrape meat off bones.
